note: Part 2 of 2: 25 items spread across the already-complete chapters s01-s11 so the track reaches exactly +20 in every type. Sections s12-s16 are in python-core.json.

items.q: Interview: 'Python me variable declaration kyun nahi hoti' — iska technically correct jawab kya hai?
items.a: Naam aur object alag cheezein hain: x = 5 se naam x us int object se bind hota hai, aur us naam ka koi fixed type nahi hota (rebinding se type badal sakta hai). Type object par hota hai, naam par nahi — isliye 'declaration' ki jagah assignment kehte hain.
items.x: Type object par hota hai, variable par nahi.

items.q: a = [1, 2]; b = a; b.append(3); print(a) — output aur wajah?
items.a: [1, 2, 3] — b = a ne naya list nahi banaya, dono naam ek hi object ko point karte hain (alias). Independent copy chahiye to a.copy() ya list(a) use karo.
items.x: Assignment object bind karta hai, copy nahi.

items.q: Project defense: 'Tumne data validation me type conversion kaise handle kiya — har jagah int() call kiya?'
items.a: Nahi — boundary par hi ek parse layer hai jo str→typed value convert karti hai aur fail par field-level error deti hai (ValueError ko message ke saath wrap karke). Andar ke code me values already typed hoti hain, isliye repeated int() calls ya silent default nahi hain.
items.x: Parse boundary par, andar typed data.

items.q: Interview: '= aur == me farq' — ek line me kaise bologe?
items.a: = assignment hai (naam ko object se bind karta hai), == equality comparison hai (values compare karta hai aur bool deta hai). Isliye if x = 5 syntax error hai, if x == 5 sahi hai.
items.x: Assignment vs comparison.

items.q: Do numbers ka safe division karo jo zero par ZeroDivisionError ki jagah None de, aur // vs / ka farq dikhao.
items.x: Integer division truncate karta hai, / float deta hai.

items.q: print('a', 'b', sep='-', end='!') ke baad next print('c') — output kya hoga?
items.a: a-b!c — sep sirf us print ke arguments ke beech lagta hai aur end newline ki jagah '!' kar deta hai, isliye agla print usi line par continue karta hai.
items.x: sep arguments par, end print ke baad.

items.q: Checkpoint: input() ke teen rules likho.
items.a: Hamesha string return karta hai (int chahiye to int() se convert karo), prompt string leta hai, aur EOF/missing input par EOFError aata hai (interactive tools me default handle karo).
items.x: String + conversion + EOF.

items.q: Checkpoint: string ke teen properties likho jo bugs rokti hain.
items.a: Immutable hai (naya object banta hai, in-place change nahi), slicing index ke hisaab se chalti hai (bounds se bahar khaali string), aur f-string me formatting expressions hote hain.
items.x: Immutable + slice-safe + f-string.

items.q: Real-world: user ke naam ko display ke liye normalize karo (extra spaces, capitalization) bina data khoye.
items.x: split() double spaces bhi saaf kar deta hai.

items.q: Ye code data ko gum kar raha hai: parts = line.split(',') phir parts[3] — kab fail hota hai aur robust fix?
items.a: Jab line me kam fields ya quoted commas hon (split naïvely todta hai). Fix: csv module use karo, ya split ke baad length check karo aur short rows ko report karke skip karo.
items.x: CSV ke liye csv module, split nahi.

items.q: Project defense: 'String parsing me tumne regex use kiya ya string methods — kyun?'
items.a: Simple fixed patterns (prefix/suffix/strip) ke liye string methods — fast, readable aur bina compile overhead. Regex sirf tab jahan pattern sach me complex hai, aur wahan named groups + precompiled pattern rakha taaki readability aur performance dono theek rahe.
items.x: Simple ke liye methods, complex ke liye regex.

items.q: Interview: 'Python me switch/case kyun nahi tha' — purane code me alternative kya hai?
items.a: Dictionary dispatch: handlers = {'a': fa, 'b': fb}; handlers.get(key, default)() — ya if/elif chain. Ye O(1) lookup deta hai aur function mapping explicitly visible hoti hai. Python 3.10+ me structural match/case bhi hai.
items.x: Dict dispatch ya match/case.

items.q: if items: wali condition empty list aur zero par kya karti hai?
items.a: Dono falsy hain, isliye else chalega. Isliye length check ki jagah truthiness chalti hai — par dhyan rahe: items = 0 aur items = [] dono falsy hain, to agar 0 valid value hai to explicitly `items is not None` likho.
items.x: Falsy vs valid zero ka farq.

items.q: Checkpoint: loop ke teen control tools likho aur ek-ek ka kaam.
items.a: break (loop turant khatam), continue (current iteration skip, loop chalu), aur for-else (loop break ke bina khatam hone par chalta hai).
items.x: Break, continue, else.

items.q: Real-world: list me se pehla valid record dhoondho aur na mile to default do (loop-else ke saath).
items.x: for-else 'mila ya nahi' ko saaf likhta hai.

items.q: List ko loop ke andar remove karte hue iterate kar rahe ho aur kuch items skip ho rahe hain. Fix?
items.a: Mutating during iteration index shift karta hai. Fix: naya list banao ([x for x in items if keep(x)]) ya reversed copy par loop chalao (pop ke liye), ya index ko manually decrement karo — comprehension sabse safe hai.
items.x: Comprehension se naya list banao.

items.q: Project defense: 'Tumne list aur generator me kahan kaunsi choose ki — kyun?'
items.a: Jab poori collection par multiple passes ya random access chahiye (reports, validation), list rakhi; jab streaming parse/transform ho aur memory constant rakhni ho, generator use kiya. Ek jagah 2GB file par list se memory blow-up dekh kar generator par shift kiya.
items.x: Passes chahiye → list, streaming → generator.

items.q: nums = [1, 2, 3]; print(nums.sort(), sorted(nums)) — dono output batao.
items.a: Pehla None (sort in-place hai aur None return karta hai), doosra [1, 2, 3] (sorted naya list return karta hai). Original list already sort ho chuki hai, isliye sorted ka output wahi dikhta hai.
items.x: sort() in-place, sorted() naya list.

items.q: Checkpoint: append, extend, insert ke output farq ek-ek line me likho.
items.a: append(x) ek item jodta hai (x list ho to poori list ek element), extend(iterable) saare items jodta hai, insert(i, x) diye index par element daalta hai (baaki shift).
items.x: Teen jodne ke tarike.

items.q: Project defense: 'Queue/stack implement karne ke liye list chuni ya deque — kyun?'
items.a: End par push/pop ke liye list O(1) hai, par index 0 se pop O(n) (poora shift). Isliye FIFO queue ke liye collections.deque use kiya (O(1) dono ends), aur stack ke liye list kaafi thi — choice access pattern par depend karti hai.
items.x: End se kaam = list, dono ends = deque.

items.q: Interview: tuple kab list se better choice hai?
items.a: Jab record fixed ho aur immutability semantic guarantee de (coordinates, config keys, dict keys), ya unpacking/return-multiple-values chahiye. List tab jab collection badhegi. Immutable hone se tuple hashable bhi hota hai (dict key ban sakta hai).
items.x: Fixed record = tuple.

items.q: Project defense: 'Function se multiple values return karte waqt tumne tuple use kiya ya dict?'
items.a: Tuple jab order natural aur caller ko position pata ho (jaise (value, error)); dict/dataclass jab fields zyada hon ya optional hon, taaki call site readable rahe (result['count'] vs result[2]). Field 3+ ho jaayein to dataclass better.
items.x: Chhote fixed returns tuple, warna named.

items.q: Checkpoint: set ke teen use-case likho.
items.a: Membership check/dedupe (unique values), set algebra (union, intersection, difference), aur dict/set keys ke liye hashable collections.
items.x: Membership + algebra + keys.

items.q: Real-world: do user lists compare karo — common users, sirf-A wale, aur sirf-B wale.
items.a:
a, b = {1, 2, 3}, {3, 4}
print('common', a & b)
print('only a', a - b)
print('only b', b - a)
print('all', a | b)
items.x: Set operators teeno jawab ek line me dete hain.

items.q: Project defense: 'Deduplicate karne ke liye set use kiya — kya order aur duplicates ka koi asar pada?'
items.a: Set order guarantee nahi karta, isliye jab output deterministic chahiye tha wahan list(dict.fromkeys(items)) use kiya (insertion order + dedupe). Set sirf wahan rakha jahan order matter nahi karta, jaise membership checks.
items.x: Order chahiye to dict.fromkeys.
